references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same argument: every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and if Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself—how then can his kingdom stand?
The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus asks how Satan can drive out Satan, explaining that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand.
The preceding context where some accuse Jesus of driving out demons by Be'elzebul, the ruler of demons—the very accusation Jesus addresses in verse 18.

The immediate continuation of Jesus' argument: if he drives out demons by Be'elzebul, by whom do their own sons drive them out? And if it is by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
The Pharisees accuse Jesus of driving out demons by the prince of demons—the same type of accusation mentioned in Luke 11:18.
Jesus warns that if they have called the master of the house Be'elzebul, how much more will they call those of his household—referring to the same name, Be'elzebul.
Jesus' preceding words that every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a house divided against itself falls—this forms the basis for the rhetorical question in verse 18.
Daniel's prophecy that God's kingdom will never be destroyed—in contrast to Satan's kingdom, which cannot stand if it is divided against itself.
